strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem for speech language models: obtaining high-quality acoustic representations with fewer codebooks. The proposed masking mechanism offers a plausible approach to redistributing information across quantizers.

The reconstruction results show useful gains. At four codebooks, Language-Codec improves PESQ and speaker similarity over both EnCodec and EnCodec+Vocos on both LibriTTS splits. Evaluation includes multiple complementary metrics and an additional LJSpeech test.

Downstream experiments cover both VALL-E and MobileSpeech. Both show improved speaker similarity, with favorable quality MOS results. The human evaluation controls text and prompts and includes 50 samples with at least 10 listeners per sample.
The manuscript provides a code/checkpoint URL and documents dataset sources, hardware, optimization settings, and parts of the downstream training procedure.
weaknesses: The principal methodological contribution is not isolated experimentally. Section 4.5 compares pretrained EnCodec/Vocos components against a system that also changes quantization, training data, and joint training. Consequently, the improvements cannot be attributed specifically to MCRVQ. An otherwise identical RVQ baseline trained on the same data is needed, alongside an experiment separating the effect of data scale.

The claimed reduction in the gap to speech language modeling is only indirectly supported. There are no quantitative measurements of per-channel information, text-conditioned token prediction difficulty, or computational savings. Table 2 also omits codebook counts and token budgets, preventing assessment of the central claim that fewer channels reduce downstream burden. Improved speaker similarity establishes a useful system-level result but does not demonstrate the proposed explanation.

Important implementation details remain unclear in the manuscript: the precise temporal mask assignment, treatment of masked positions, fusion of quantizer outputs, and cumulative residual calculation are insufficiently specified. Equation 5 does not resolve these ambiguities. Codebook sizes, decoder dimensions, loss weights, and the downstream codec configuration also need explicit documentation. Additionally, 20,000 of the 50,000 training hours are internal data, limiting independent retraining despite the reported release.

There are concrete reporting inconsistencies and overstated comparisons. Table 3 reports LJSpeech UTMOS values of 3.7091/3.8955 for Language-Codec, whereas Table 4 reports 3.8549/4.0127 for the same four/eight-codebook settings, without explanation. Claims of comprehensive superiority also exceed the results: SpeechTokenizer has higher UTMOS on several settings, and eight-codebook Vocos exceeds Language-Codec on LJSpeech UTMOS.

The uncertainty of the downstream improvements is insufficiently established. Table 2 does not define its ± values or report paired statistical comparisons; several MOS differences over EnCodec+Vocos are small. WER and prosody change little, so conclusions should distinguish demonstrated speaker-similarity gains from uncertain improvements elsewhere. Together with the missing controlled ablation and implementation specification, these issues warrant revision before a clear Findings recommendation.
